extracted.intended_audience: novelists, serious creative writers, and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling narrative method and point of view in novels (pictorial vs dramatic approaches), including when to use first person, how to authenticate the narrator, and how to balance narration and enacted scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the point of view / 'bring its own recognisances'
rubrics_metrics.description: “The book that we read has no such support; it must bring its own recognisances.... At any moment [the mind that knows the story and the eye that sees it] may be questioned, and the only way to silence the question is somehow to make the mind and the eye objective, to make them facts in the story.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always make the narrative vantage-point verifiable within the book. If the story requires a selecting/seeing eye, the author must authenticate whose mind/eye is doing the selecting—either by dramatizing that seer or by otherwise making its presence an observable fact. Failure to do so leaves the point of view unaccountable and weakens the book's authority; examples and remedies are discussed via Thackeray, Flaubert, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the narrator ('make a drama of the narrator himself')
rubrics_metrics.description: “It would then be like a play within a play... the recorder stands outside and away from his book... the activity that is proceeding in his mind is not in itself an element in the effect of the book, as it might be. So long as the recorder stands outside... the author must supply his view, but he might treat his view as though it were in its turn a piece of action.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat acts of remembering, interpreting, or judging as dramatic actions—give the narrator visible activity and placement in the scene so that his viewpoint both authenticates the picture and adds independent interest. Examples: Thackeray's Esmond makes the narrator a visible actor; the 'calling up' of recollection can be staged as an inner drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conspicuous omniscient-author intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: “The fiction of [an obvious authorial presence] drags in the omniscient author and may make him exceedingly conspicuous... It makes for a kind of thinness in the general impression... [and] may contribute towards an air of ineffectiveness in a story.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial commentary that cannot be verified from within the story-world (an intrusive omniscient voice) risks creating thinness and loss of authority, especially on rereading. Only tolerate such intrusion if the author's personality/charm justifies it; otherwise minimize or dramatize the author's presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first person to localize and individualize point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: “The characterized ‘I’ is substituted for the loose and general ‘I’ of the author; the loss of freedom is more than repaid by the more salient effect of the picture. Precision, individuality is given to it by this pair of eyes, known and named, through which the reader sees it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person narration is an effective device in pictorial novels to fix a field of vision, provide tone and colour, and give the picture a definite edge. It supplies a named vantage-point and personal colour that a detached omniscient ‘I’ cannot. Examples: Esmond, David Copperfield, Meredith's uses and limits are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economize drama—reserve scenes for essential moments
rubrics_metrics.description: “Drama is the novelist’s highest light... to use it prodigally where it is not needed is to lessen its force where it is essential. And so the economical procedure would be to hoard it rather, reserving it for important occasions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat enacted scenes as a scarce, high-value resource. Overusing scenes in everyday, familiar novels wastes their power; save dramatic enactment for climaxes or moments that require intensity so the impact is not diluted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance pictorial sweep and dramatic scene; manage the two methods
rubrics_metrics.description: “The quality of a novelist appears very clearly in his management of the two, how he guides the story into the scene, how he picks it out of the scene, a richer and fuller story than it was before, and proceeds with his narrative.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novelist should master both broad, pictorial narration (covering ranges of life and experience) and concentrated dramatic scenes, and guide transitions between them skillfully. Different writers tend toward one method (Fielding, Balzac, Eliot = pictorial; Tolstoy, Dostoevsky = scenic) but excellence lies in the handling of both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first-person/autobiographical form to unify episodic or retrospective narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: “Autobiography—... the hero gives the story an indefeasible unity by the mere act of telling it. His career may not seem to hang together logically, artistically; but every part of it is at least united with every part by the coincidence of its all belonging to one man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the novel is primarily a long retrospective or a succession of adventures (a panorama of memory), first-person narration can knit disparate episodes into a coherent whole and make formlessness feel like authentic shape (example: David Copperfield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of first-person when subject is the narrator's inner history
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the man in the book is expected to make a picture of himself, a searching and elaborate portrait, then the limit of his capacity is touched and passed; or rather there is a better method, one of finer capacity... drama ought to be used.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the novel's central subject is the narrator's own moral/emotional development, relying solely on his report (autobiography) may be inadequate. In such cases the narrator's inner life should be dramatized so readers can judge change for themselves (Meredith's Harry Richmond is used as the cautionary example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the narrator's spatial/relational position measurable (show the line of sight)
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the point of view is definitely included in the book, when it can be recognized and verified there, then every side of the book is equally wrought and fashioned... Now, [when] Beatrix appears, we know who it is that so sees her, and we know where the seer is placed; his line of sight... is measurable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify where the seer stands in relation to the scene/characters—showing the angle, distance, or situation makes perceived characters more solid and objective (contrast Becky in Vanity Fair with Beatrix in Esmond).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift from narration to enactment as emphasis demands
rubrics_metrics.description: “Inevitably, as the plot thickens and the climax approaches... narration gives place to enactment, the train of events to the particular episode, the broad picture to the dramatic scene.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a plot moves toward emphasis or climax, move from summarizing narration into fully enacted scenes. Use enactment to make important impressions forceful and immediate; reserve such shifts for moments that demand dramatic attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unverifiable authorial information—'show' what the reader can test
rubrics_metrics.description: “[Turgenev] will draw the reader aside and pour into his ear a flow of information... information which will never have its due weight with the reader, because it reposes upon nothing that he can test for himself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements or background that come only from an external tell-all narrator (with no means for the reader to verify) lack persuasive weight. Prefer showing, dramatizing, or embedding such information in observable actions or character interactions so the reader can assess it.
